TILDE: Teacher-in-the-Loop Distillation from Embodied Foundation Models

Yuxiang Lu  Yantong Liu*  Jinghua Hou  Xueli Sun  Ruihua Han Zhe Liu  Hengshuang Zhao The University of Hong Kong https://hku-sail.github.io/TILDE ††thanks: Equal Contribution
Abstract

Large-scale action pretraining equips Embodied Foundation Models (EFMs) with strong manipulation capabilities, with particular strengths in generalization and closed-loop robustness, but reproducing such pretraining requires substantial robot data and computation. To transfer these capabilities from pretrained EFMs to policies without action pretraining, we introduce TILDE (Teacher-In-the-Loop Distillation from EFMs), which synergizes on-policy distillation at student-induced states with learning from teacher-executed recovery trajectories. We further propose AutoDAgger, an autonomous data aggregation pipeline in which a robotic reward model is utilized to monitor task progress and trigger teacher intervention, thereby collecting recovery experience without human monitoring or manual control. AutoDAgger accelerates recovery-trajectory collection by more than 2×2\times compared with the human-in-the-loop method. By unifying learning from demonstrations, on-policy teacher supervision, and teacher’s corrective behavior, TILDE improves task performance by up to 4.1×4.1\times over behavior cloning across three real-world tasks and supports effective cross-architecture distillation.

1 Introduction

Embodied Foundation Models (EFMs), including Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models (Zhang et al., 2025a; Shao et al., 2025; Ma et al., 2024; Sapkota et al., 2025), have demonstrated remarkable manipulation capabilities and generalization. However, these capabilities often rely on action pretraining on large-scale robot datasets (Bu et al., 2025; Padalkar et al., 2024; Walke et al., 2023; Khazatsky et al., 2024), making it costly to endow new policy architectures, particularly efficient models, with comparable capabilities (Yu et al., 2025; Guan et al., 2025). Reproducing foundation-scale pretraining requires access to sufficiently diverse, high-quality robot data and substantial computational resources, which is prohibitively expensive in many research and deployment settings.

Policies without large-scale action pretraining (Lin et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2026a; Community, 2026) can still achieve competitive performance on standard simulation benchmarks such as LIBERO-Spatial and LIBERO-Object (Liu et al., 2023). However, our pilot study suggests that this apparent parity does not consistently extend to more challenging settings. As shown in Figure 1, substantially larger gaps emerge on long-horizon tasks in LIBERO-10, under visual and robot-initial-state perturbations (Fei et al., 2025), and in real-world tasks. These observations are consistent with action pretraining providing benefits beyond nominal action prediction, particularly improved closed-loop robustness under challenging and out-of-distribution conditions. This motivates a natural question: Can such capabilities be transferred from a pretrained EFM to a student policy without repeating expensive action pretraining?

Policy distillation offers an intuitive route by transferring teacher knowledge in a task-specific domain (Rusu et al., 2015; Dong et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2025b). However, for closed-loop policies, effective distillation depends not only on what actions are supervised, but also on where supervision is provided. When distillation is restricted to a fixed demonstration dataset (Figure 1(a)), supervision remains concentrated on the nominal distribution. During closed-loop deployment, compounding student errors and environmental stochasticity can drive the policy into out-of-distribution states. This distribution mismatch between training and inference leaves the student insufficiently prepared to handle execution deviations (Yan et al., 2026; Hu et al., 2026).

Interactive imitation learning mitigates this mismatch by querying expert supervision at states induced by the learner (Ross et al., 2011). In On-Policy Distillation (OPD) (Agarwal et al., 2024; Agarwal et al., 2023), the student interacts with the environment while the teacher provides action targets at student-visited states (Figure 1(b)). This expands supervision to student-induced rollout states, but the queried teacher actions are not executed (Zhong et al., 2026; Wan et al., 2026). Consequently, OPD does not observe the subsequent states that would arise following the teacher’s correction. Human-in-the-loop approaches such as HG-DAgger (Kelly et al., 2019) (Figure 1(c)) can collect recovery trajectories but require continuous human monitoring and teleoperated takeover (Murray et al., 2026; Xu et al., 2025), severely limiting data scalability.

To address these limitations, we introduce TILDE (Teacher-In-the-Loop Distillation from EFMs), a policy distillation framework that transfers teacher knowledge over three complementary data distributions: human demonstration, student-induced rollouts, and recovery trajectories (Figure 1(d)). Central to TILDE is AutoDAgger, an autonomous teacher-in-the-loop data aggregation pipeline. An off-the-shelf robotic reward model monitors student execution, while the execution manager uses its feedback to trigger intervention, after which the EFM teacher directly takes control and executes a recovery trajectory toward task completion. Automated progress monitoring removes the need for expensive human oversight, while teacher policy takeover avoids the reaction and teleoperation overhead of human intervention, substantially enhancing recovery-data collection throughput.

Given the aggregated data, TILDE applies supervision according to the sample source. Offline demonstrations and teacher recovery trajectories provide both behavior-cloning targets from executed actions and teacher distillation targets, while student rollout states use on-policy teacher supervision only. Importantly, all distillation is performed directly in the common action space and requires no alignment of internal representations, allowing the framework to accommodate heterogeneous teacher and student architectures.

Our contributions are summarized as follows:

  1. 1.

    We formulate policy distillation from a distributional perspective and propose the TILDE framework, which jointly transfers teacher knowledge over offline demonstrations, student-induced rollouts, and teacher-generated recovery experience.

  2. 2.

    We introduce AutoDAgger, an autonomous teacher-in-the-loop data aggregation pipeline that expands the training distribution through automatic task monitoring and teacher takeover, enabling efficient recovery-data collection while bypassing expensive human involvement.

  3. 3.

    Extensive experiments on real-world manipulation tasks demonstrate that TILDE improves student performance by up to 4.1×4.1\times over behavior cloning, consistently outperforms offline and on-policy distillation, and enables effective cross-architecture capability transfer.

2 Related Work

Embodied Foundation Models.

Recent advances in large-scale robot learning have given rise to Embodied Foundation Models (EFMs) that integrate visual perception, language understanding, and low-level control, showing impressive performance across a broad spectrum of dexterous tasks and improved generalization to diverse environments (Zhang et al., 2025a; Shao et al., 2025; Ma et al., 2024; Xu et al., 2024b). Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models directly map multimodal observations and language instructions to robot actions (Intelligence et al., 2025a; Intelligence et al., 2026; Bjorck et al., 2025; Zheng et al., 2026; Fan et al., 2026; Lu et al., 2026). An emerging alternative is the World Action Model (WAM), which jointly models future world states and robot actions, rather than relying solely on reactive observation-to-action prediction (Ye et al., 2026; Li et al., 2026; Yuan et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026b). Despite their strong capabilities, training such foundation models from scratch requires substantial data and computational resources. Our work instead studies how the capabilities of a pretrained EFM can be transferred to a student policy without repeating foundation-scale pretraining.

Policy Distillation.

Knowledge Distillation (KD) transfers predictions or representations from a teacher to a smaller student and is widely used for model compression and capability transfer (Hinton et al., 2015; Buciluǎ et al., 2006). Policy distillation extends this paradigm to robot learning (Rusu et al., 2015; Torne et al., 2024; Dong et al., 2025; Shao et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2025b), with recent advances leveraging foundation models as teachers (Jülg et al., 2025). Existing methods perform distillation through model-level alignment (Jeon et al., 2026; Ye et al., 2025) or teacher-generated data and supervision (Shi et al., 2026; Xiao et al., 2026; Xu et al., 2024a). On-Policy Distillation (OPD) further queries teacher supervision on student-induced states rather than relying solely on a fixed offline dataset (Agarwal et al., 2024; Agarwal et al., 2023), providing corrective signals where the student tends to encounter uncertainty or make mistakes (Zhong et al., 2026; Wan et al., 2026). Our method extends OPD by executing teacher takeover after intervention, thereby collecting the subsequent recovery trajectory and providing direct supervision for returning from off-nominal states to successful task execution.

Interactive Imitation Learning.

Imitation learning suffers from distribution shift when the learned policy encounters states absent from expert demonstrations. Interactive imitation learning mitigates this issue by querying an expert on learner-induced states and iteratively aggregating the resulting supervision (Ross et al., 2011). Subsequent methods reduce expert queries using predicted novice–expert discrepancy (Hoque et al., 2021b), policy uncertainty (Menda et al., 2019; Kelly et al., 2019; Zurbrügg et al., 2026), or estimates of state novelty and task risk (Cronrath et al., 2018; Hoque et al., 2021a). However, these approaches generally depend on policy-specific techniques or continuous human oversight, and still request human teleoperation for corrective takeover on physical robots (Murray et al., 2026; Xu et al., 2025). In contrast, we propose a novel data aggregation framework that automatically detects intervention needs and executes corrective actions, substantially reducing the human-effort bottleneck in interactive data collection.

3 Methodology

3.1 Preliminaries

Task Formulation.

We consider standard language-conditioned robotic manipulation with action-chunking policies (Chi et al., 2023). Given an observation state 𝒔{\bm{s}} comprising RGB images and robot proprioception, together with a language instruction 𝒍{\bm{l}}, a policy π\pi predicts an action chunk:

π⁡(𝒔,𝒍)=𝑨=[𝒂1,…,𝒂H],\pi({\bm{s}},{\bm{l}})={\bm{A}}=[{\bm{a}}_{1},\dots,{\bm{a}}_{H}], (1)

where HH denotes the policy’s prediction horizon and 𝒂h{\bm{a}}_{h} is the hh-th action in the chunk. During closed-loop execution, the policy is repeatedly queried using updated observations.

DAgger.

Dataset Aggregation (DAgger) (Ross et al., 2011) is an interactive imitation learning algorithm that addresses the distribution shift between offline demonstrations 𝒟demo\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{demo}} and learner rollouts 𝒟roll\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{roll}} by collecting expert action labels at learner-induced states. In the representative human-in-the-loop variants, the human expert monitors the execution progress and takes control when the learner’s behavior requires correction by providing recovery actions 𝒂⋆{\bm{a}}^{\star} at the encountered observation 𝒔{\bm{s}}. The resulting labeled samples (𝒔,𝒍,𝒂⋆)({\bm{s}},{\bm{l}},{\bm{a}}^{\star}) are added to an aggregated dataset 𝒟rec\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{rec}}, which is used to update the learner through behavior cloning.

3.2 Overview

TILDE transfers task-relevant capabilities from a capable and robust teacher policy πT\pi_{T} to a student policy πS\pi_{S}. With a base human demonstration dataset 𝒟demo\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{demo}}, the teacher policy is finetuned from the pretrained EFM on the dataset to adapt to specific embodiment and target task, and remains frozen in the framework. The student policy is initialized from a pretrained backbone (e.g., VLM in a VLA model) but receives no robot action pretraining, and is trained on 𝒟demo\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{demo}} using standard behavior cloning. TILDE consists of two stages: (1) In the AutoDAgger data collection, the student executes the task while a task monitor estimates progress and an execution manager triggers teacher intervention when needed. The teacher takes over to perform recovery, and only episodes with confirmed teacher recovery are combined with the student rollout and added to the aggregated dataset. (2) During action distillation, the student learns from teacher supervision on student-visited states, together with corrective trajectories and existing demonstrations, combining knowledge distillation with imitation learning of recorded expert behaviors.

3.3 AutoDAgger

To reduce human supervision and collect informative correction data more efficiently, we propose AutoDAgger, an autonomous teacher-in-the-loop pipeline that monitors student execution, detects task-level failures, triggers teacher takeover, and retains successfully recovered trajectories for subsequent policy improvement.

Task Monitor.

We employ a general-purpose robotic reward model RR as a policy-independent task monitor. We index monitor updates by t=1,2,…t=1,2,\ldots and denote the timestamp of the tt-th update by τt\tau_{t}. At each update, the monitor evaluates Kt≤NframeK_{t}\leq N_{\mathrm{frame}} observations stored in a bounded visual-history buffer, denoted by 𝒐1:Kt{\bm{o}}_{1:K_{t}}, together with the language instruction 𝒍{\bm{l}}, to predict sequences of task progress and success probability:

(𝒑^1:Kt,𝒒^1:Kt)=R(𝒐1:Kt,𝒍).\left(\hat{{\bm{p}}}_{1:K_{t}},\hat{{\bm{q}}}_{1:K_{t}}\right)=R\left({{\bm{o}}}_{1:K_{t}},{\bm{l}}\right). (2)

We extract the most recent predictions and clip them to [0,1][0,1]:

pt=clip(𝒑^1:Kt[−1],0,1),qt=clip(𝒒^1:Kt[−1],0,1),p_{t}=\operatorname{clip}\!\left(\hat{{\bm{p}}}_{1:K_{t}}[-1],0,1\right),\quad q_{t}=\operatorname{clip}\!\left(\hat{{\bm{q}}}_{1:K_{t}}[-1],0,1\right), (3)

where ptp_{t} and qtq_{t} represent the predicted current task progress and success probability, respectively.

Execution Manager.

The execution manager coordinates policy execution, teacher intervention, and data selection based on information from the task monitor. Each episode begins with the student policy, while detected failures trigger teacher takeover. To identify failures, we check for sustained progress stagnation when the task is not currently predicted to be successful. Specifically, to avoid interpreting small fluctuations in the predicted progress ptp_{t} as task advancement, we maintain a reference progress value p¯t\bar{p}_{t}, updated only when ptp_{t} exceeds the previous reference by a margin ϵp\epsilon_{p}. The meaningful-progress indicator gtg_{t} and reference update are defined as

gt=𝕀[pt>p¯t−1+ϵp],p¯t={pt,gt=1,p¯t−1,gt=0.g_{t}=\mathbb{I}\!\left[p_{t}>\bar{p}_{t-1}+\epsilon_{p}\right],\quad\bar{p}_{t}=\begin{cases}p_{t},&g_{t}=1,\\ \bar{p}_{t-1},&g_{t}=0.\end{cases} (4)

The execution manager interprets qt>θsq_{t}>\theta_{s} as an instantaneous prediction of task success. We regard either meaningful progress or such a success prediction as evidence of valid execution and track the timestamp of the most recent evidence:

τtvalid={τt,gt=1∨qt>θs,τt−1valid,otherwise.\tau_{t}^{\mathrm{valid}}=\begin{cases}\tau_{t},&g_{t}=1\;\lor\;q_{t}>\theta_{s},\\ \tau_{t-1}^{\mathrm{valid}},&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases} (5)

A failure is detected when the elapsed time since the last valid execution reaches TfailT_{\mathrm{fail}} and the current success probability does not exceed θs\theta_{s}:

Δt=τt−τtvalid,Ft=𝕀[Δt≥Tfail∧qt≤θs].\Delta_{t}=\tau_{t}-\tau_{t}^{\mathrm{valid}},\quad F_{t}=\mathbb{I}\!\left[\Delta_{t}\geq T_{\mathrm{fail}}\;\land\;q_{t}\leq\theta_{s}\right]. (6)

When Ft=1F_{t}=1 during student execution, the manager immediately halts the student and transfers control to the teacher policy. The same monitoring mechanism is applied during teacher execution. Task completion is confirmed when consecutive qtq_{t} predictions remain above θs\theta_{s} for at least TsuccT_{\mathrm{succ}}, with any prediction at or below the threshold resetting the success timer. If teacher recovery fails, the episode is discarded. Otherwise, the student rollout and teacher recovery segment are retained as a combined trajectory and aggregated for subsequent policy training.

3.4 Distillation Objective

Given the trajectories collected by AutoDAgger, TILDE trains the student from three complementary sources of experience: offline demonstrations 𝒟demo\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{demo}}, states visited during student rollouts 𝒟roll\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{roll}}, and teacher-executed recovery trajectories 𝒟rec\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{rec}}. For an observation-instruction pair (𝒔,𝒍)({\bm{s}},{\bm{l}}), we perform distillation directly in the action space using

ℒKD​(𝒔,𝒍)=ℓS​(𝒔,𝒍,sg⁡[𝑨T]),\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{KD}}({\bm{s}},{\bm{l}})=\ell_{S}\left({\bm{s}},{\bm{l}};\operatorname{sg}\!\left[{\bm{A}}_{T}\right]\right), (7)

where sg⁡[⋅]\operatorname{sg}[\cdot] stops gradients through the frozen teacher and ℓS\ell_{S} denotes the original action-generation objective used by the student, instantiated with the teacher-predicted action chunk 𝑨T=πT​(𝒔,𝒍){\bm{A}}_{T}=\pi_{T}({\bm{s}},{\bm{l}}) as the target. Since supervision is imposed only on action outputs, TILDE does not require the teacher and student to share similar architectures or intermediate representations.

For samples from either offline demonstrations or recovery trajectories, the action actually executed in the environment is available. Let 𝑨E{\bm{A}}_{E} denote this recorded action chunk. We therefore combine behavior cloning from the executed action with distillation from the teacher prediction:

ℒexec​(𝒔,𝒍,𝑨E)=ℓS​(𝒔,𝒍,𝑨E)+λKD​ℒKD​(𝒔,𝒍),(𝒔,𝒍,𝑨E)∈𝒟demo∪𝒟rec,\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{exec}}({\bm{s}},{\bm{l}},{\bm{A}}_{E})=\ell_{S}({\bm{s}},{\bm{l}};{\bm{A}}_{E})+\lambda_{\mathrm{KD}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{KD}}({\bm{s}},{\bm{l}}),\quad({\bm{s}},{\bm{l}},{\bm{A}}_{E})\in\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{demo}}\cup\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{rec}}, (8)

where λKD\lambda_{\mathrm{KD}} is the weight of distillation loss. In contrast, as samples from 𝒟roll\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{roll}} contain states visited by the student, we apply only the distillation objective:

ℒroll​(𝒔,𝒍)=λKD​ℒKD​(𝒔,𝒍),(𝒔,𝒍)∈𝒟roll.\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{roll}}({\bm{s}},{\bm{l}})=\lambda_{\mathrm{KD}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{KD}}({\bm{s}},{\bm{l}}),\quad({\bm{s}},{\bm{l}})\in\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{roll}}. (9)

Overall, the training loss is selected according to the source of each sample. This formulation exposes the student to three complementary data distributions. Offline demonstrations provide supervision on in-domain expert behavior, student rollouts provide teacher corrections at student-induced states, and recovery trajectories supply the subsequent observations induced by executing the teacher’s corrections.

4 Experiments

4.1 Experimental Setup

Tasks and Evaluation.

We conduct real-world experiments with 7-DoF AgileX PiperX robot arms on three manipulation tasks: (1) “Fold Dishcloth”: folding a dishcloth in half twice and placing it at a target location toward the front left, testing deformable object manipulation; (2) “Pick Pen”: picking up one to three pens and placing them in a cup, testing precise manipulation across object locations; and (3) “Pick Beverage”: picking up a beverage and placing it in a paper box, focusing on generalization across objects and locations. We collect 200 human demonstration episodes for Fold Dishcloth and 100 for each of the other two tasks.

We evaluate each policy on the same predefined test cases, with fixed object types, positions, and orientations: 12 trials for Fold Dishcloth, 27 for Pick Pen, and 30 for Pick Beverage. We define fine-grained evaluation metrics to enable a more precise assessment of policy performance, with the detailed scoring criteria provided in Appendix A.2. Scores are averaged across sub-steps and evaluation trials, while the success rate (SR), which measures complete task success, is reported as a complementary metric.

Implementation Details.

We obtain the teacher by finetuning the pretrained π0.5\pi_{0.5} VLA model (Intelligence et al., 2025b) on the human demonstrations for each task. Unless otherwise specified, the student employs the same architecture as π0.5\pi_{0.5} but receives no action pretraining: its VLM backbone is initialized from PaliGemma (Beyer et al., 2024), while the action expert is trained from scratch. The task monitor in AutoDAgger leverages the off-the-shelf robotic reward model Robometer (Liang et al., 2026) without task-specific finetuning.

Baselines and Training Protocol.

We compare TILDE with three training paradigms: standard behavior cloning (BC) (Bain & Sammut, 1995; Pomerleau, 1988), offline distillation, and On-Policy Distillation (OPD). BC learns from recorded human actions, offline distillation additionally uses teacher action targets on demonstration states, and OPD further incorporates teacher supervision at student-rollout states. TILDE unifies learning from three complementary data distributions. Unless otherwise stated, comparisons use a shared pool of collected AutoDAgger data, containing 30 successfully recovered and retained episodes per task.

4.2 Main Results

Figure 3 shows that offline distillation yields only modest improvements over BC, as teacher supervision remains confined to the demonstration distribution. OPD yields further gains by mitigating distribution mismatch through adding teacher supervision at student-rollout states. TILDE achieves scores of 63.9, 80.6, and 69.2 on Fold Dishcloth, Pick Pen, and Pick Beverage, respectively, outperforming all evaluated baselines on each task. These scores are approximately 3.07×3.07\times, 2.18×2.18\times, and 4.14×4.14\times those of the BC baseline, substantially narrowing the observed student–teacher performance gap. These consistent improvements support the value of learning from recovery data in addition to teacher action targets at student-induced states.

4.3 Analysis

Ablation Study.

We first examine the contributions of student-rollout supervision and teacher-executed recovery trajectories using offline distillation as the common baseline. As shown in Figure 4 (left), adding either source improves performance on all three tasks, while combining both produces the highest scores. These results indicate that each source improves performance when the other is already present, supporting their complementary roles in transferring teacher behavior.

Figure 4 (right) further analyzes the supervision used on demonstrations and recovery trajectories. Recovery BC adds imitation of the teacher’s recorded actions to conventional BC and improves performance on all three tasks. Recovery Distill additionally applies knowledge distillation to both demonstration and recovery samples, achieving further advantages.

Recovery from Failures.

To directly assess whether recovery trajectories from teacher policy improve closed-loop correction behavior, we construct a standardized recovery-state evaluation with a common set of 12 distinct error states on Fold Dishcloth. Each state deviates from nominal execution and requires corrective behavior before the task can be completed. As shown in Table 2, the BC baseline succeeds from only 4 out of 12 states, while offline distillation and OPD improve this result slightly to 5/12. TILDE succeeds in 8 cases, compared with 9/12 for the pretrained teacher. These results support the value of learning from the subsequent states generated by executing teacher corrections, where TILDE transfers substantially stronger recovery capability.

Scaling with AutoDAgger Data.

Table 2 studies how performance scales with the amount of AutoDAgger data. Starting from a score of 27.8 with offline distillation on the human demonstration dataset, the student improves to 63.9, 65.3, and 77.8 after aggregating 30, 60, and 90 AutoDAgger episodes, respectively. The corresponding success rates exhibit a similar upward trend, indicating consistent improvement. Notably, with 90 AutoDAgger episodes, the student reaches a score of 77.8, narrowing the gap to the teacher score of 87.5. These results suggest that TILDE could benefit further from continued scaling of interactive recovery data.

Quality and Efficiency of AutoDAgger Data.

Table 3 compares augmenting the original dataset with the same number of additional human teleoperation episodes or AutoDAgger episodes per task. Under BC, AutoDAgger data yield scores of 48.6, 63.0, 50.0 on Fold Dishcloth, Pick Pen, and Pick Beverage, compared with 27.8, 45.4, and 44.2 using additional human demonstrations. With distillation enabled, the AutoDAgger configuration achieves scores of 63.9, 80.6, and 69.2 across the three tasks, substantially outperforming the additional-demonstration configuration. These results suggest that AutoDAgger data provide more effective supervision than conventional expert demonstrations, which typically consist of trajectories that directly lead to task success. In contrast, AutoDAgger provides corrective supervision at student-induced states that are rarely encountered during standard demonstration collection, while also enabling on-policy distillation to more effectively leverage the teacher’s knowledge.

We further compare AutoDAgger with HG-DAgger (Kelly et al., 2019), a representative human-in-the-loop data aggregation method, in terms of downstream policy performance, data collection efficiency, and intervention success. As shown in Table 4, AutoDAgger substantially reduces the time required to collect recovery trajectories across all three tasks. This improvement primarily stems from direct takeover by the teacher policy. Once an intervention is triggered, the teacher can immediately generate and execute corrective actions from the current state, whereas human teleoperation incurs additional reaction and control overhead.

Despite replacing human intervention with automated teacher takeover, AutoDAgger achieves recovery success rates comparable to those of HG-DAgger. Recovery is not always successful for either method, as some failure states are inherently difficult to recover from. Importantly, HG-DAgger requires a human operator to continuously monitor execution and manually take over when intervention is needed, whereas AutoDAgger automates both processes. By eliminating human involvement during data collection while substantially increasing collection throughput, AutoDAgger provides a more scalable alternative to human-in-the-loop data aggregation.

Faster recovery offers an opportunity to close the small performance gap through additional autonomous data collection. On Fold Dishcloth, increasing the AutoDAgger dataset to 60 episodes raises the score to 65.3 (Table 2), matching HG-DAgger with 30 episodes. Combined with the 2.53×\times recovery-time speedup, this result suggests that AutoDAgger can use its collection efficiency to improve downstream performance within a comparable time budget.

Cross-architecture Distillation.

We investigate whether TILDE can transfer capabilities across heterogeneous model architectures. Since our approach performs distillation purely through action-space alignment rather than intermediate feature alignment, the teacher and student can employ different architectures and action-generation mechanisms. We use SmolVLA (Shukor et al., 2025) without action pretraining as an efficient student policy and distill knowledge from the π0.5\pi_{0.5} teacher on the LIBERO benchmark. As shown in Table 6, TILDE consistently improves the student and outperforms conventional offline distillation. On the long-horizon LIBERO-10 suite, success increases from 64.6% to 79.6%, consistent with our motivation to transfer capabilities needed in more challenging settings. These results validate the broader applicability of our framework and suggest that pretrained EFMs can serve as reusable teachers for new policy architectures.

Validation of Task Monitor.

Since AutoDAgger triggers interventions based on task execution estimates from a task monitor implemented with the Robometer reward model, we further evaluate its ability to distinguish successful and failed rollouts on the LIBERO benchmark. We collect 200 SmolVLA rollout episodes on each suite and compare the model’s success predictions with the ground-truth outcomes provided by the simulator. As shown in Table 6, Robometer achieves strong performance across the four suites, although recall decreases on the more challenging LIBERO-10 tasks. These results support its use as an off-the-shelf, policy-independent task monitor for AutoDAgger without task-specific finetuning.

5 Conclusion

In this work, we study how capabilities acquired through large-scale action pretraining can be transferred from pretrained EFMs to new student policies without repeating foundation-scale pretraining. TILDE combines teacher supervision at student-induced states with teacher-executed recovery trajectories, covering both corrective actions and the subsequent recovery-state distribution. AutoDAgger enables this process without human monitoring or takeover through task monitoring and execution management. Across three real-world manipulation tasks, TILDE consistently improves over behavior cloning, offline distillation, and conventional on-policy distillation, while AutoDAgger collects recovery data more than 2×\times faster than HG-DAgger. Cross-architecture experiments with SmolVLA further validate capability transfer to heterogeneous student policies.

Appendix

We provide the following contents in the appendix:

  • •

    Appendix A provides implementation details of AutoDAgger, real-world experiments, simulation benchmarks, training configurations, and robot deployment.

  • •

    Appendix B presents additional experimental results, including failure-detection evaluation, statistics, and visualizations of the AutoDAgger data-collection process.

  • •

    Appendix C discusses limitations and potential directions for future work.

Appendix A Additional Implementation Details

A.1 AutoDAgger

Methodological Details.

Let nn index incoming policy-inference requests, and let 𝒐n{\bm{o}}_{n} denote the front-camera observation accompanying the nn-th request. Each observation is appended to a bounded visual-history buffer. Whenever the buffer exceeds NframeN_{\mathrm{frame}} observations, its contents are downsampled by retaining NframeN_{\mathrm{frame}} evenly spaced observations. We denote the resulting buffer after processing 𝒐n{\bm{o}}_{n} by ℬn\mathcal{B}_{n}.

Each monitor output received by AutoDAgger constitutes a task-monitor update, indexed by t=1,2,…t=1,2,\ldots, with reception timestamp τt\tau_{t}. Let ntn_{t} denote the index of the policy-inference request at which the buffer snapshot associated with update tt is submitted for evaluation. The corresponding monitor input is

𝒐~(t)1:Kt=ℬnt,Kt=|ℬnt|≤Nframe.\widetilde{{\bm{o}}}^{(t)}_{1:K_{t}}=\mathcal{B}_{n_{t}},\quad K_{t}=\left|\mathcal{B}_{n_{t}}\right|\leq N_{\mathrm{frame}}. (10)

For notational simplicity, the main text denotes this snapshot by 𝒐1:Kt{\bm{o}}_{1:K_{t}}. Monitoring requests are submitted in response to incoming policy observations, subject to a minimum interval of τmon\tau_{\mathrm{mon}} seconds between consecutive submissions. Request submission and monitor evaluation are performed asynchronously without blocking policy inference.

At the beginning of each episode, AutoDAgger clears the visual-history buffer and prediction records, resets the progress reference and temporal state, and removes pending monitoring requests. We initialize τ0valid=τ0\tau_{0}^{\mathrm{valid}}=\tau_{0}, where τ0\tau_{0} denotes the episode start time. Since no progress reference is available before the first monitor update, we initialize p¯1=p1\bar{p}_{1}=p_{1}, set g1=1g_{1}=1, and assign τ1valid=τ1\tau_{1}^{\mathrm{valid}}=\tau_{1}. Failure detection begins after this initialization. For t≥2t\geq 2, the progress reference and valid-execution timestamp follow Equations 4 and 5.

Between monitor updates, the execution manager continuously evaluates stagnation using the current wall-clock time and the latest valid-execution timestamp. This allows the execution manager to trigger intervention as soon as the stagnation duration reaches TfailT_{\mathrm{fail}}, without waiting for another monitor output. At monitor-update timestamps, the continuous-time check reduces to Equation 6.

The execution manager continuously polls the task monitor associated with the active policy. During student execution, the student monitor is active while the teacher monitor remains idle. Upon detecting student failure, the manager immediately stops the robot and clears the action buffer and observation window to invalidate pending student actions. Control is then transferred to the teacher policy, and monitoring restarts with a fresh state. The task-monitor index, progress reference, and temporal variables are maintained separately for each policy and reinitialized at takeover. Robot execution resumes only after a teacher action chunk becomes available, preventing residual student actions from being executed after the transfer.

During teacher recovery, the manager applies the same failure-detection mechanism, using the teacher’s monitoring state and temporal thresholds. Monitoring continues until recovery is successfully confirmed or teacher failure is detected. If teacher recovery fails, the episode is discarded. Otherwise, the student rollout and teacher recovery segment are retained as a combined trajectory for subsequent policy training. Episodes successfully completed by the student are also discarded, as AutoDAgger specifically targets recovery-data collection.

Hyperparameter Setup.

Across all experiments, we fix Nframe=8N_{\mathrm{frame}}=8, τmon=1​s\tau_{\mathrm{mon}}=1\,\mathrm{s}, ϵp=0.05\epsilon_{p}=0.05, and θs=0.5\theta_{s}=0.5. The buffer capacity NframeN_{\mathrm{frame}} balances temporal context against monitoring cost, while τmon\tau_{\mathrm{mon}} controls the minimum interval between monitoring requests. The progress margin ϵp\epsilon_{p} prevents minor fluctuations in predicted progress from being treated as meaningful advancement, and θs\theta_{s} determines the threshold for predicted task success.

We configure the temporal thresholds for failure detection and success confirmation separately for each task and policy. The failure timeout TfailT_{\mathrm{fail}} specifies the maximum duration of execution stagnation before a policy is classified as failed, provided that task success is not currently predicted.

The same success-confirmation criterion is applied to both student execution and teacher recovery. Let τtsucc\tau_{t}^{\mathrm{succ}} denote the reception timestamp of the first output in the current uninterrupted sequence of monitor predictions satisfying qt>θsq_{t}>\theta_{s}. This timestamp is initialized when a new sequence begins and remains unchanged while subsequent predictions stay above the threshold. Any prediction at or below the threshold resets the success timer. Success is evaluated only upon receipt of a new monitor output and is confirmed at update tt when

qt>θs∧τt−τtsucc≥Tsucc.q_{t}>\theta_{s}\;\land\;\tau_{t}-\tau_{t}^{\mathrm{succ}}\geq T_{\mathrm{succ}}. (11)

This criterion requires temporally consistent success predictions, reducing false completion detections caused by transient prediction spikes. The temporal thresholds used during autonomous data collection are summarized in Table 7, with all values reported in seconds.

We use different temporal thresholds for the student and teacher to accommodate their execution characteristics. A shorter TfailT_{\mathrm{fail}} enables earlier detection of student failures and timely teacher intervention, reducing the risk of further deviation from recoverable states. In contrast, a longer teacher timeout allows sufficient time to recover from student-induced off-nominal states. Thresholds also vary across tasks to account for differences in execution dynamics and expected duration. For example, folding a dishcloth involves contact-rich manipulation and may exhibit temporary pauses during valid execution, whereas picking tasks typically involve more temporally compact and visually apparent progress.

A.2 Real-world Experiments

Hardware Setup. We conduct our real-robot experiments on an AgileX PiperX dual-arm robot platform, as illustrated in Figure 5, following the leader-follower teleoperation design of ALOHA-style systems (Zhao et al., 2023; Fu et al., 2024). The platform consists of four 7-DoF (6 joints + 1 gripper) PiperX arms: two leader arms operated by a human demonstrator and two corresponding follower arms that reproduce the leader commands during data collection and execute policy-generated actions during autonomous inference. The visual sensing system comprises one front-facing Intel RealSense D455 camera and two Intel RealSense D435 wrist cameras, with one wrist camera mounted on each follower arm.

Tasks. We evaluate our method on three real-robot manipulation tasks: “Fold Dishcloth”, “Pick Pen”, and “Pick Beverage”. These tasks cover deformable-object manipulation, precision grasping, and object relocation. Illustrations of the three tasks are provided in Figure 6.

The language instructions for the tasks are:

  • •

    Fold Dishcloth: “Fold the dishcloth in half twice, then place it in the position slightly to the front and left.”

  • •

    Pick Pen: “Pick up the scattered pens one by one and place them in the yellow cup.”

  • •

    Pick Beverage: “Pick up the beverage and put it in the paper box.”

Evaluation Protocol.

Each method is evaluated using a fixed number of real-robot rollouts per task: 12 trials for Fold Dishcloth, 27 trials for Pick Pen, and 30 trials for Pick Beverage. We use predefined test configurations, including fixed object categories and controlled variations in object position and orientation, and keep these configurations as consistent as practically possible across all evaluated methods. A rollout is considered successful only if the complete task is accomplished within the maximum episode length without human intervention.

In addition to binary task success, we report a fine-grained success score to capture both partial task completion and execution quality under a limited real-robot evaluation budget. Each task is decomposed into semantically meaningful stages. Each stage receives a score of 00, 0.50.5, or 11, corresponding to failure, partial completion or successful completion after repeated attempts, and successful completion in a single attempt, including immediate recovery from minor execution issues, respectively. The task-level score is computed by averaging over all stages and evaluation rollouts, and then multiplied by 100 for better display. The scoring criteria are as follows:

  1. 1.

    Fold Dishcloth

    • •

      Stage 1: Folding the dishcloth in half from left to right

      • –

        0: The robot fails to complete the fold after multiple attempts.

      • –

        0.5: The robot completes the fold after several attempts or demonstrates partial recovery from an execution error during the process.

      • –

        1: The robot completes the fold in a single attempt, including cases in which it immediately recovers from minor issues such as a flipped corner.

    • •

      Stage 2: Folding the dishcloth in half a second time, from bottom to top

      • –

        0: The robot fails to complete the second fold after multiple attempts.

      • –

        0.5: The robot completes the second fold after several attempts or demonstrates partial recovery from an execution error during the process.

      • –

        1: The robot completes the second fold in a single attempt, including cases in which it immediately recovers from minor issues such as a flipped corner.

    • •

      Stage 3: Picking up the folded dishcloth and placing it in the front-left target region

      • –

        0: The robot fails to pick up and place the folded dishcloth after multiple attempts.

      • –

        0.5: The robot completes the pick-and-place operation after several attempts or demonstrates partial recovery from an execution error during the process.

      • –

        1: The robot completes the pick-and-place operation in a single attempt.

  2. 2.

    Pick Pen

    • •

      Stage 1: Grasping the pen

      • –

        0: The robot fails to grasp the pen.

      • –

        0.5: The robot grasps the pen after repeated attempts or recovers from an unsuccessful grasp.

      • –

        1: The robot grasps the pen correctly on the first attempt.

    • •

      Stage 2: Placing the pen into the cup

      • –

        0: The pen is not placed into the cup or is dropped outside it.

      • –

        0.5: The pen is placed into the cup after a recovery attempt or with substantial contact against the cup.

      • –

        1: The robot directly places the pen into the cup without requiring recovery.

    • •

      For trials containing multiple pens, the two-stage scoring procedure is applied independently to each pen.

      • –

A.3 Simulation Benchmarks

LIBERO.

The LIBERO benchmark (Liu et al., 2023) has four task suites—Spatial, Object, Goal, and 10 (Long)—each emphasizing different manipulation capabilities. We train a single policy jointly across all four suites. For π0.5\pi_{0.5}, VLA-Adapter-Pro, and SmolVLA, we use the dataset released by OpenVLA11 1 HuggingFace: openvla/modified_libero_rlds (Kim et al., 2024) and convert it to the LeRobot format (Cadene et al., 2026). For X-VLA, we instead use the HDF5-format dataset released by the X-VLA authors22 2 HuggingFace: 2toINF/Libero-XVLA-format, which represents actions in the EE6D action space. Each suite consists of 10 tasks, and each task is evaluated over 50 rollouts.

LIBERO-Plus.

LIBERO-Plus (Fei et al., 2025) extends LIBERO with seven dimensions of visual and configuration perturbations. In our pilot study (Figure 1), we evaluate the “Background” setting, which perturbs scene and surface appearance, and the “Robot” setting, which varies the manipulator’s initial pose. These settings contain 1,076 and 1,550 task instances, respectively. The evaluations are performed using checkpoints trained exclusively on the original LIBERO data, thereby measuring out-of-distribution generalization under environmental and embodiment perturbations.

A.4 Training Setup

We train π0.5\pi_{0.5}33 3 GitHub: Physical-Intelligence/openpi, X-VLA44 4 GitHub: 2toinf/X-VLA, VLA-Adapter55 5 GitHub: OpenHelix-Team/VLA-Adapter, and SmolVLA66 6 GitHub: huggingface/lerobot based on their official codebases, with modifications to support our training pipeline and data formats. For the action-pretraining-free variants of π0.5\pi_{0.5} and X-VLA, we initialize the model from VLM backbones: PaliGemma (Beyer et al., 2024) for π0.5\pi_{0.5}, and Florence-2-large (Xiao et al., 2024) for X-VLA, while training the action experts from scratch.

We follow the default or recommended training configurations for each model, with the key hyperparameters summarized in Table 8 and Table 9. During training, samples are drawn randomly from the pooled training datasets without additional dataset balancing, and the training loss for each sample is determined by its data source. The supervision applied to each training variant is summarized in Table 10. We set the distillation loss weight λKD=1\lambda_{\mathrm{KD}}=1 for all experiments. For real-robot experiments, demonstrations are recorded in absolute joint space at 30FPS and converted to relative joint actions by subtracting the corresponding proprioceptive states if needed.

For AutoDAgger data collection, the student collection policy is first trained on 𝒟demo\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{demo}} using behavior cloning only. We then perform AutoDAgger collection using this fixed BC baseline. After collection, we reinitialize the student and train on the aggregated dataset.

During distillation, when both the teacher and student use the π0.5\pi_{0.5} architecture, we compute the distillation loss ℒKD​(𝒔,𝒍)\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{KD}}({\bm{s}},{\bm{l}}) by directly matching their flow-matching velocity predictions using shared noise samples. When the student uses a different architecture, such as SmolVLA, we instead use the teacher’s fully-denoised action predictions as supervision targets and train the student with the same imitation learning objective used for ground-truth actions.

All models are trained on 8 NVIDIA A800 GPUs with 80GB VRAM. Training takes approximately 1–2 days for π0.5\pi_{0.5} and less than one day for the other models.

A.5 Robot Deployment Setup

We deploy the policy and task-monitor models on a workstation equipped with NVIDIA RTX 4090 GPU. The inference latency is 80.0±1.680.0\pm 1.6ms for π0.5\pi_{0.5} and 266.9±0.5266.9\pm 0.5ms for the task monitor Robometer. The robot-side client runs on ROS at a fixed control frequency of 30Hz. We employ asynchronous inference together with temporal ensembling to enable continuous control and smooth the action trajectories.

A.6 Cross-architecture Distillation Setup

For the cross-architecture experiment in Table 6, we follow the same collection and training protocol described above. We use π0.5\pi_{0.5} as the teacher and SmolVLA as the student, which is first trained by behavior cloning on the LIBERO dataset. We then use this BC student for AutoDAgger collection and train TILDE using the resulting student-rollout and teacher-recovery data together with the demonstrations.

Appendix B Additional Experimental Results

B.1 Validation of Task Monitor on Real-world Rollouts

We further evaluate the task monitor and execution manager using 20 real-robot rollouts, consisting of 10 student rollouts and 10 teacher rollouts. Ground-truth outcomes are manually determined according to whether the corresponding policy successfully completes the task. Among the student rollouts, two are successful and eight are failed; among the teacher rollouts, eight are successful and two are failed. The complete evaluation set is therefore balanced, containing 10 successful and 10 failed trajectories.

In Table 11, Positive denotes that the monitoring system predicts task success, while Negative denotes that it detects task failure. True and False refer to ground-truth task success and failure, respectively. The monitoring system correctly identifies 8 of the 10 successful trajectories and 9 of the 10 failed trajectories, yielding an overall accuracy of 85%85\%. The two FNs indicate that the monitor adopts a conservative criterion for confirming task success. This conservative behavior is useful for teacher recovery verification, where a trajectory may complete the task only after multiple corrective attempts. Rejecting such trajectories reduces success recall but helps prevent lower-quality recovery data from entering the training set. Overall, the monitoring system achieves a precision of 88.9%88.9\%, a recall of 80.0%80.0\%, and an F1 score of 84.2%84.2\%. Although the evaluation set is limited by the cost of real-robot experiments, these results indicate that the task monitor provides a practical signal for triggering teacher takeover and verifying recovery outcomes.

B.2 Experimental Result Statistics

We supplement the performance statistics of experiments in the main text in Table 12, Table 13, Table 14, and Table 15.

B.3 Visualization of AutoDAgger Collection

We visualize representative AutoDAgger collection trajectories for Fold Dishcloth, Pick Pen, and Pick Beverage tasks in Figure 7. Before intervention, the predicted task progress initially increases during student execution but subsequently stagnates, while the success probability remains well below θs=0.5\theta_{s}=0.5. The execution manager consequently detects the combination of sustained progress stagnation and low success probability, triggering teacher takeover at the red-bordered frames. Following takeover, the predicted progress may decrease temporarily as the teacher corrects the student-induced state. It subsequently resumes increasing as recovery proceeds, reaching 0.8690.869, 0.8140.814, and 0.8470.847 for the three tasks. Meanwhile, the success probability remains low during most of the recovery process and rises above θs\theta_{s} only near task completion, reaching 0.8440.844, 0.5820.582, and 0.9260.926, respectively.

Appendix C Limitations and Future Work

Despite the improved student performance demonstrated by TILDE, several limitations remain. First, TILDE is evaluated with a single round of AutoDAgger collection followed by student training, rather than iterative data aggregation. Extending the experiments to alternate between policy updates and subsequent rounds of AutoDAgger could progressively expose the student to increasingly relevant failure and recovery states. Second, AutoDAgger relies on the accuracy of the task monitor and the recoverability of the teacher policy; incorrect intervention decisions or failure states beyond the teacher’s capability may reduce the quality or efficiency of collected data. More robust task monitoring and adaptive intervention strategies are therefore promising directions. Finally, our experimental evaluation focuses on a limited set of real-world tasks, simulation benchmarks, and teacher–student architectures. Future work will scale TILDE to broader tasks, embodiments, and heterogeneous policy families, and investigate how closely student policies can approach pretrained EFMs with continued autonomous data aggregation and distillation.
